segments.say: At the start of a relationship, everything feels new and exciting. Every conversation is a discovery. Every outing is an adventure. But as the years pass, routines settle in. The same restaurants. The same evenings on the sofa. The same conversations. And for many couples, a quiet kind of boredom can creep in.

First, I want to say that routine in a relationship is not a bad thing. Familiar rituals, shared habits, the comfort of knowing someone deeply, these are some of the most precious parts of a long relationship. But a complete lack of novelty may, for some couples, gradually lead to a sense of flatness.

The psychologist Arthur Aron and his colleagues studied this in a set of experiments published in two thousand. Couples came to the lab and took part in an activity together. Some did a novel, slightly challenging task. For example, crawling across mats while bound together at the wrist and ankle, carrying a cushion between them without using their hands. Others did a more mundane, easy task.

show.where: Stony Brook University, published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2000
show.what: Couples took part in either a novel, mildly challenging activity together, or a more mundane activity, and then rated their relationship satisfaction.

segments.say: The couples who did the novel, challenging activity together reported greater relationship satisfaction afterwards, compared with those who did the mundane task. Aron suggested that sharing new and exciting experiences may help couples associate that excitement with each other, bringing back some of the energy of the early days.

Aron and his colleagues proposed what they called the self expansion model. The idea is that people are motivated to grow, to learn, to expand who they are. Early in a relationship, getting to know a new person expands us rapidly. Later, that growth slows. Doing new things together can restart that sense of growth, and of discovery.

This doesn't require grand adventures. Trying a new recipe together. Visiting a new neighborhood. Taking a class. Playing a new game. Going on a different walk. Small doses of novelty, shared, may help keep a relationship feeling alive. Remember the habit research, and how novelty breaks autopilot. The same seems true for couples.

Another gentle approach is renewed curiosity. Even after many years, there is always more to discover about another person. Their dreams, their memories, their changing opinions. Asking new questions, really listening, can make a familiar person feel fascinating again. Aron is also known for a set of questions designed to build closeness between strangers, which some couples use to deepen their connection too.

The same ideas apply to friendships. Long friendships can fall into comfortable patterns, which is lovely. But adding a new shared experience now and then, a trip, a project, a new activity, can bring fresh energy and new memories to share.

And it's worth remembering that comfortable silence with someone you love isn't the same as boredom. Sitting together quietly, reading, watching the sunset, can be a deep form of intimacy. The difference, once again, is in how it feels. Restless and empty, or peaceful and connected.

show.cap: Not every quiet moment is boredom.

segments.say: I find this research quietly romantic. It suggests that love is kept alive not only by grand gestures, but by small shared adventures. New experiences together, creating new memories together. And those memories become part of the story you share, the story of who you are, together.

So here's what we've learned about boredom in relationships. Long relationships naturally settle into routines. In experiments, couples who did novel, challenging activities together reported greater satisfaction. Shared new experiences can restart a sense of growth and discovery. And comfortable, peaceful silence with someone you love is not boredom at all.

show.title: Boredom in love
items: Doing new things together restarts growth

segments.say: And these days, whenever boredom threatens, whether at work, at home, or in a relationship, there's a device in our pockets ready to fill the gap. Has the smartphone ended boredom? Or changed it? Let's look at that next.
